column1: Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 12?
column2: Simon Mace of City Rail Link and Simon Fenton of AECOM, the Link Alliance Construction Phase Services manager.

column1: What is the length of the City Rail Link tunnels?
column2: 3.45 km of twin underground tunnels.

column1: How many stations does CRL involve, and what is the total project cost?
column2: Four new and upgraded stations, at a total project cost of .5 billion NZD.

column1: What capacity does CRL unlock?
column2: It doubles Auckland's rail capacity to 54,000 passengers per hour at peak.

column1: How deep is CRL at its deepest point?
column2: 45 metres below the city.

column1: What is CRL's asset life, and what has been future-proofed?
column2: A 100-year asset life, future-proofed to run nine-car trains - 50% longer than the current 3- and 6-car trains.

column1: When was CRL first proposed and when did construction start?
column2: It was nominated over 100 years ago and construction started about a decade ago.

column1: Why is CRL's maximum gradient 3.5% rather than the network's 2.5%?
column2: Because stations must be perfectly flat, so the flat sections force the intervening track to be steeper to cover the topography from Waitemata up to Maungawhau.

column1: What is unusual about the turnouts at Maungawhau?
column2: They are underground, which is something you would never normally do, but the layout forced it - a unique arrangement in New Zealand.

column1: Which CRL benefit is a network effect rather than a direct effect?
column2: Doubling the number of people living within a 30-minute public transport commute of the city centre - the value comes from the connection, not the asset.

column1: What social legacy did CRL claim?
column2: The upskilling of workers who worked on the project, with up to 2,000 people employed on site during construction.

column1: Which CRL contract was by far the largest?
column2: Contract three, the Link Alliance works covering stations, tunnels and rail systems.

column1: Why was the timing of the Commercial Bay tunnels critical?
column2: It was the one opportunity to use the route up to Albert Street - if the tunnels had not been built while the tower was being built, they could never have been added later.

column1: How were tunnels built under the heritage Chief Post Office?
column2: The building was supported on a temporary structure, the tunnels were excavated and built underneath, then the building was lowered back onto the new support.

column1: What do the CRL station names reflect?
column2: The cultural narrative of the areas they serve, mirrored in the architectural design, with the Maori creation story depicted in the stations.

column1: What does the name Te Waihorotiu relate to?
column2: The stream which still runs underneath Queen Street.

column1: What is notable about the name Karanga-a-Hape?
column2: It is a grammatical correction of Karangahape as commonly written.

column1: Define an alliance contract.
column2: A relationship-style arrangement bringing together the client, contractor and consultant team to deliver the project, sharing all the risks and all the rewards.

column1: How does an alliance differ from a design and construct contract?
column2: In D&C the constructor goes away, provides a lump sum and must deliver within that budget; in an alliance risk and reward are shared across client, contractor and consultants.

column1: Who made up the Link Alliance?
column2: City Rail Link as client, constructors Vinci Grands Projets, Downer and Soletanche Bachy, and consultants Tonkin and Taylor, AECOM and WSP.

column1: Which named sub-consultants worked on CRL?
column2: Grimshaw as architects and Jacobs on earthing and bonding specialisms.

column1: What did Simon Mace find when he revisited the 2015 CRL business case?
column2: The strategic case objectives were the same objectives being delivered eleven years later - the case for change held even though costs moved.

column1: Name the five Better Business Cases as the CRL speaker described them.
column2: Strategic - why would you do it; economic - identifying the best value option; commercial - how it would be delivered; financial - benefits, costs and BCR; management - how you would manage and deliver it.

column1: What are wider economic benefits?
column2: Additional economic output created because businesses can recruit better staff, workers have more opportunities, and businesses become more productive.

column1: What is preliminary engineering design for?
column2: Enough engineering design to inform a cost estimate.

column1: What is the premise of the second half of Lecture 12?
column2: That consultancy engineering doesn't end with a drawing - there is life after the drawing, between design and construction.

column1: What is Construction Phase Services?
column2: The middleman function between the design team and the construction team, navigating the interface between them.

column1: Name the three pillars of Construction Phase Services.
column2: Quality including protection of the design intent, technical clarifications through RFIs, and managing change.

column1: Why is Construction Phase Services needed?
column2: Because of unknowns like utilities and ground conditions, change, re-sequencing and interface changes, material supply availability, and contributing to safety, wellbeing, performance and quality.

column1: Who signs a PS1?
column2: The design team, based on the drawings.

column1: Who signs a PS2?
column2: An independent checker - another design consultant reviewing the drawings, depending on project scale.

column1: Who signs a PS3?
column2: The construction team, confirming they built what is on the drawings.

column1: Who signs a PS4, and on what basis?
column2: Construction Phase Services, based on their observation that the construction team have done a good job and it is good to go.

column1: What qualification is required to sign a design producer statement?
column2: You must be a chartered engineer, through Engineering New Zealand.

column1: What is the design certificate chain, and how does it differ from producer statements?
column2: DC1 to DC4, covering project and client requirements, whereas producer statements are focused on building consent sign-off - one satisfies the client, the other the council.

column1: What is an inspection test plan?
column2: A start-to-finish guide showing how the quality expectations of the project are met for a particular work function, written by the constructor from the designer's specification.

column1: What does the accumulated ITP evidence allow?
column2: Signing the PS4 - it becomes the consolidated body of information behind the sign-off.

column1: What is a hold point?
column2: A mandatory stop of works until the CPS team has inspected and approved, used where there is a point of no return.

column1: What is a witness point?
column2: An inspection CPS may choose to attend, based on confidence in the constructor's performance.

column1: How does the number of witness points change?
column2: It flexes with observed performance - fewer if the constructor is doing well, more if they are struggling. It is based on relationships.

column1: Why do hold points exist?
column2: Because once concrete is poured or kilometres of cable are pulled, it is very difficult to go back in time.

column1: Describe diaphragm wall construction as used at K Road.
column2: A hydrofraise drills from the surface to 43 metres, the excavation is filled with bentonite to retain the ground, a reinforcement cage of about 30 metres is dropped in, concrete is tremied from the bottom displacing the bentonite, and the ground is later excavated out from underneath.

column1: What did CPS check during diaphragm wall construction?
column2: The method statement, the reinforcement cages, the bentonite consistency, the depth and cleanliness of the base, the concrete mix and strengths, and the finished wall after excavation.

column1: What does CM5 monitoring mean?
column2: The highest level of construction monitoring, meaning CPS is on site full time to see everything.

column1: What is a non-conformance report?
column2: A record of something going wrong that identifies the problem, records its location, assigns responsibility for the fix, and agrees the corrective action.

column1: Why do constructors dislike NCRs, and why do they matter?
column2: They feel like criticism of workmanship, but they ensure the team learns so the same mistake is not repeated, and they provide an audit trail captured in as-builts, change management and handover documentation.

column1: Give three ways ground and site conditions departed from the drawings on CRL.
column2: Assumed consistent ground produced pressure changes; work passed under live motorways causing vibration; and old steel strands from the Aotea Centre's temporary works had to be de-stressed before the TBM could pass.

column1: What is the rule about utilities?
column2: Utilities are never in the right place - they have never been as-built correctly, and the Auckland city centre is a bird's nest of them.

column1: Give the cable specification cascade example.
column2: Cable specs are based on assumed electrical equipment; if the equipment changes and draws more power, the cable sizes must be changed to suit.

column1: What happened to material supply assumptions on CRL?
column2: A global pandemic brought lockdowns and supply chain disruption - as the speaker put it, they don't care about our programme.

column1: Why does Simon Fenton call communication a hard skill?
column2: Because it can be learned, and many project problems come down to poor communication and relationships rather than technical ability.

column1: What is the formal communication channel on a project, and why does it exist?
column2: Requests for information recorded in a document management system, so that decisions are captured formally as an audit trail.

column1: Give the RFI cycle.
column2: Raise an RFI, someone reviews it, a response is issued, the change is implemented, and someone confirms implementation.

column1: State the golden rule for a good RFI response.
column2: Explain the design intent - the why, not just the outcome.

column1: Give the box-out example of a good versus poor RFI response.
column2: A poor response is simply no; a good one explains that there is a lot of tension in that area, the bars carry tensile loads, and moving them would strain the underside of the beam and risk failure.

column1: What does explaining the design intent buy you?
column2: The contractor understands the constraint and can generate their own alternatives, rather than simply coming back again.

column1: What five things beyond code must a balanced engineering decision weigh?
column2: Is it safe, can we afford it, does it fit the programme, what quality do we expect, and what does the client want.

column1: Give the formula for good engineering judgement.
column2: Experience plus evidence plus common sense.

column1: Why is engineering judgement most needed on site?
column2: Because in a design office you have time, but on site something has happened, something needs to change, and they need an answer now.

column1: Work through the damaged architectural panel example.
column2: Fixing it needs scaffold that must be got in, a worker over a 20-metre drop, significant cost, risk of damaging something else, and the station opens next week - so the case for fixing it falls away.

column1: Name the steps of the change management process.
column2: Identify the change, assess risks, impacts, access, safety and cost, develop options and recommendations, seek approval scaled to the size of the change, issue a design site instruction, then construct and verify.

column1: How does change approval scale?
column2: A minor change may need only a minor review; a bigger change may go back to an independent certifier.

column1: What is a DSI?
column2: A design site instruction - the formal document capturing a change, issued through the document management system.

column1: How many as-built drawings were produced for CRL?
How many client requirements had to be incorporated into CRL designs?
column2: Just over 20,000 individual requirement lines.

column1: How many PS4 sets, building consents and engineering plan approvals did CRL have?
column2: 109 PS4 sets, 74 building consents and 42 engineering plan approvals.

column1: When did CRL reach practical completion?
column2: 30 June.

column1: Why can't project assurance be done retrospectively?
column2: Because you cannot make it up at the end - you cannot find photos that were never taken.

column1: Give three CRL wow facts.
column2: 244,000 cubic metres of concrete, 70,000 tonnes of steel reinforcement, 24 million hours worked, and 2,056 kilometres of cables.

column1: What was the CRL yellow card scheme?
column2: A safety scheme where anyone on site could issue a yellow card to flag something either unsafe or safe - 29,234 were submitted.

column1: How much CO2 did CRL's sustainability initiatives save?
column2: Around 20,000 tonnes.

column1: What BIM level of development did CRL achieve?
column2: LOD 500 - a fully certified, verified and checked model reflecting everything including maintenance requirements.

column1: What second use did the BIM model have beyond design?
column2: Stakeholder management - it was used to win buy-in from mana whenua groups and politicians visiting the design office.

column1: How many people worked on the CRL project?
column2: About 15,000.

column1: What whakatauki closed the lecture?
column2: He aha te mea nui o te ao? He tangata, he tangata, he tangata - what is the most important thing in the world? It is people, it is people, it is people.
